facts.fact_text: In 2007 Mr Kasparov (the first applicant), together with other individuals representing a coalition of opposition groups, intended to take part in an anti-government rally to campaign before the forthcoming parliamentary elections.
The demonstration became known as the March of Dissenters.
The March of Dissenters was organised by three individuals, none of whom are applicants in the present case.
On 30 March 2007 the three organisers of the March of Dissenters submitted notice of a public demonstration to the mayor of Moscow.
The notice indicated that a meeting would be held at 12 noon on 14 April 2007 in Novopushkinskiy Park.
The notice indicated that the meeting would last until 1.30 p.m.
The notice indicated that the meeting would be followed by a march via Tverskaya Street and Okhotnyy Ryad Street to Teatralnaya Square.
The notice indicated that the march was to end at 2 p.m.
The organisers estimated that about 2,000 people would take part in the event.

The notice stated that the proposed demonstration was intended "to express the demands of Russian citizens for the urgent reinstatement of the full scope of citizens' electoral rights, through the abolition of the legislative amendments of recent years".
According to the Government, on 14 April 2007 at about 11.40 a.m. groups of people started gathering near Pushkinskaya Square.
According to the Government, a group of about twenty persons, including the first eight applicants, started marching down Tverskaya Street while shouting anti-government slogans on 14 April 2007.
According to the Government, the total number of people who took part in the unauthorised march on 14 April 2007 was about fifty.
According to the Government, the first eight applicants were arrested as they tried to pass from Tverskaya Street onto Red Square on 14 April 2007.
The applicants claimed that they had not staged a demonstration in Tverskaya Street, but had happened to be there for different reasons.

Mr Kasparov (the first applicant), Mr Tarasov (the second applicant) and Mr Toropov (the fifth applicant) claimed that at 12 noon on 14 April 2007 they had been walking peacefully down Tverskaya Street towards the place of the authorised meeting at the Griboyedov monument.
The applicants did not specify the number of people walking alongside them on 14 April 2007.
The applicants claimed that their way had been barred by the riot police who were blocking off several streets in central Moscow on 14 April 2007.

The applicants claimed that all pedestrians, both aspiring protesters and unsuspecting passers-by, had been pushed back, surrounded and indiscriminately beaten up by the riot police before being arrested and taken in police vans to different police stations on 14 April 2007.
Mr Stelmakh (the sixth applicant) claimed that he had not been heading to a meeting but had been walking down Tverskaya Street with his friends on 14 April 2007.
Mr Stelmakh (the sixth applicant) claimed that when he saw the riot police dispersing a crowd and arresting people he had dropped into the "Russkoye Bistro" café on Tverskaya Street.
Mr Stelmakh (the sixth applicant) claimed that he was arrested at about 12 noon in the "Russkoye Bistro" café on Tverskaya Street on 14 April 2007.
Mr Kharlamov (the third applicant) claimed that he had had no intention of participating in a public event on 14 April 2007.
Mr Kharlamov (the third applicant) claimed that he had been arrested when he came out of a shop near Pushkinskaya Square after having collected his mobile phone, which was being repaired.
Mr Kalashnikov (the fourth applicant) claimed that he had been arrested when he was heading to a local McDonald's restaurant to meet a friend on 14 April 2007.
Mr Orel (the seventh applicant) submitted that he had been heading to McDonald's on 14 April 2007 but could not get there because the street was closed off by the riot police.
Mr Orel (the seventh applicant) claimed that he had dropped into the "Russkoye Bistro" café on Tverskaya Street, where he had been arrested on 14 April 2007.
Mr Melikhov (the eighth applicant) said that he had been heading to McDonald's on 14 April 2007 but could not get there and had been arrested in Tverskaya Street.
The applicants claimed that there had been at least thirty other people in the police van, all of whom had been arrested at the same time as the applicants on 14 April 2007.
Ms Chelysheva (the ninth applicant) alleged that on 14 April 2007 she had been heading to the meeting at the Griboyedov monument.
Ms Chelysheva (the ninth applicant) alleged that at Sretenskiye Vorota Square she and other pedestrians had been attacked by a unit of the riot police on 14 April 2007.
Ms Chelysheva (the ninth applicant) alleged that she had seen a policeman hitting a man with a truncheon and had intervened to try to stop the beating.
Ms Chelysheva (the ninth applicant) alleged that a policeman had kicked her on her left leg.
Ms Chelysheva (the ninth applicant) alleged that she had been badly hurt and therefore could not go to the meeting at the Griboyedov monument on 14 April 2007.

On 5 April 2007 the Department for Liaison with Security Authorities of the Moscow Government informed the organisers that the event was liable to disrupt the functioning of urban services and the movement of passers-by.

The Department for Liaison with Security Authorities of the Moscow Government informed the organisers that authorisation could only be granted for a meeting at the foot of the Griboyedov monument on Chistoprudnyy Boulevard between 12 noon and 1.30 p.m.
The authorised meeting at the foot of the Griboyedov monument on Chistoprudnyy Boulevard was at a different location in central Moscow from the originally proposed venue.

The Department for Liaison with Security Authorities of the Moscow Government informed the organisers that the number of participants at the authorised meeting could not exceed 1,000, the maximum capacity of the venue.
No march was authorised by the Department for Liaison with Security Authorities of the Moscow Government.
On 6 April 2007 the organisers resubmitted the notice, proposing four alternative routes for the march, all in central Moscow.
On 6 April 2007 the organisers agreed to limit the number of participants to 1,000.
On 10 April 2007 the Department for Liaison with Security Authorities of the Moscow Government informed the organisers that none of the four alternative routes could be accepted.
The Department for Liaison with Security Authorities of the Moscow Government rejected the four alternative routes for the same reasons as the refusal of the original proposal.
The Department for Liaison with Security Authorities of the Moscow Government suggested that the organisers hold the event at an aeronautical club in one of the Moscow suburbs.
Documents submitted by the Government reveal that on 14 April 2007 the Moscow police were reinforced by special units of the riot police (OMON).
The OMON units reinforcing the Moscow police on 14 April 2007 were brought in specially from twenty-nine regions of Russia.
The stated purpose of bringing in OMON units from twenty-nine regions of Russia on 14 April 2007 was "to protect public order and security" on that day.

After his arrest on 14 April 2007 Mr Kasparov (the first applicant) was taken to the police station and was then brought before the Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District of Moscow.
Mr Kasparov (the first applicant) was charged with a breach of the established procedure for conducting public assemblies, an offence under Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The hearing of the administrative case against Mr Kasparov (the first applicant) was fixed for 5.30 p.m. on 14 April 2007.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District of Moscow noted the insignificant volume of the case file (five pages) and decided to hold the hearing on 14 April 2007, having postponed it first by forty-five minutes and then by an additional twenty minutes.
At 6.30 p.m. on 14 April 2007 the Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District of Moscow examined the charges against Mr Kasparov (the first applicant).
The applicants alleged that no members of the public had been allowed in the courtroom during the hearing on 14 April 2007, as the building had been cordoned off by the police.
Mr Kasparov's (the first applicant's) counsel, Ms Moskalenko, filed a motion to have the hearing opened to the public.
The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District of Moscow issued a decision stating that the hearing was open to the public.
At the beginning of the hearing on 14 April 2007, Mr Kasparov (the first applicant) filed a motion to call and examine six eyewitnesses, four of whom had been arrested at the same time as him.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District of Moscow rejected the motion to call eyewitnesses, holding that it was premature to call witnesses before the applicant and the police had been questioned.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District of Moscow examined the police report, according to which Mr Kasparov (the first applicant) had been arrested at 1.30 p.m. while "walking in a big group of people shouting anti-government slogans".
The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District of Moscow questioned Mr I., the policeman who had arrested Mr Kasparov (the first applicant) and drawn up the report.

Mr I. testified that because of the public manifestations expected to take place between 12 noon and 4 p.m. on 14 April 2007 he had received an instruction to safeguard public order at 19 Tverskaya Street, in particular to stop any organised groups of people heading in the direction of Red Square.
Mr I. testified that Mr Kasparov (the first applicant) had been walking in a group of about fifty to sixty people on 14 April 2007.

Mr I. testified that, following instructions to disperse the unauthorised demonstration which was threatening to spill over into the security perimeter of Red Square, he had arrested Mr Kasparov (the first applicant).
Mr Kasparov (the first applicant) claimed that the policeman Mr I. had given the wrong place and time of the arrest.
Mr Kasparov (the first applicant) reiterated the request to question the eyewitnesses, stating that the persons in question were waiting outside the court and were ready to be called.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District of Moscow rejected the motion to call eyewitnesses on the grounds that the persons concerned had not been mentioned in the police report and that the facts were sufficiently clear to determine the charges.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District of Moscow accepted the version of events put forward by the police, finding that Mr I.'s testimony was credible because he was performing his professional duties, had not been acquainted with the applicant, had no reason to slander him, and was a party with no vested interest.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District of Moscow referred to the Moscow authorities' decision of 5 April 2007 and concluded that on 14 April 2007 Mr Kasparov (the first applicant) had attempted to take part in an unauthorised demonstration at 19 Tverskaya Street, where he had been arrested.

Mr Kasparov (the first applicant) was found to have acted in breach of the regulations on holding demonstrations and was convicted of an administrative offence under Article 20.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
Mr Kasparov (the first applicant) was ordered to pay a fine of 1,000 Russian roubles (about 25 euros).
Mr Kasparov (the first applicant) appealed to the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow against his conviction.
Mr Kasparov (the first applicant) contested the facts as established at first instance in his appeal to the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow.
Mr Kasparov (the first applicant) claimed in his appeal that the hearing had not been held in public.
Mr Kasparov (the first applicant) alleged in his appeal that he had not been given a chance to prepare his defence or to present his case adequately.
On 14 May 2007 the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow examined Mr Kasparov's (the first applicant's) appeal.

On 14 May 2007 the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow upheld the first-instance judgment against Mr Kasparov (the first applicant), reiterating that he had participated in an unauthorised demonstration and had been marching in a group of people chanting anti-government slogans.
The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow noted that there had been no proof that the first-instance hearing had not been held in public.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow noted that there had been no proof that Mr Kasparov (the first applicant) had not been given sufficient time to prepare his defence, since he had had two hours to do so.
The administrative proceedings concerning the second to eighth applicants were conducted at first instance by the Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District of Moscow.

The second to eighth applicants were each individually convicted of having breached the procedure for the conduct of public assemblies, an administrative offence under Article 20.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The second to eighth applicants were each ordered to pay a fine of 1,000 Russian roubles.
During the trial, the second to eighth applicants all contested the police reports, in particular as regards the time and circumstances of their arrest.
During the trial, the second to eighth applicants all requested the Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District of Moscow to call and examine eyewitnesses.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District of Moscow found that the facts were sufficiently established in each of the second to eighth applicants' cases and rejected the requests to call eyewitnesses.

The decisions and reasons given by the Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District of Moscow in the second to eighth applicants' cases were essentially the same as in Mr Kasparov's (the first applicant's) case.
Mr Toropov's (the fifth applicant's) case was examined in his absence and in the absence of his lawyer.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District of Moscow rejected a motion lodged by Mr Toropov (the fifth applicant) for the proceedings to be adjourned, finding that it was possible to proceed without the applicant and his lawyer.
The first-instance judgments in the second, third, fourth and sixth applicants' cases were given on 16 April 2007.
The first-instance judgment in Mr Toropov's (the fifth applicant's) case was given on 22 May 2007.
The first-instance judgments in the seventh and eighth applicants' cases were given on 25 April 2007.
The second to eighth applicants subsequently appealed unsuccessfully to the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow.
The reasons given by the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow on appeal in the second to eighth applicants' cases were essentially the same as in Mr Kasparov's (the first applicant's) case.
The appeal decisions in the second, third, fourth, sixth, seventh and eighth applicants' cases were given on 14 May 2007.
The appeal decision in Mr Toropov's (the fifth applicant's) case was given on 11 July 2007.

On 16 April 2007 Ms Chelysheva (the ninth applicant) filed a complaint with the Moscow prosecutor's office requesting that criminal proceedings be brought against the policemen who had used force against her.
On 6 July 2007 the Meshchanskiy Inter-District Prosecutor's Office decided to dispense with a criminal investigation into the incident involving Ms Chelysheva (the ninth applicant).
On 18 March 2011 the Meshchanskiy Inter-District Prosecutor's Office quashed its decision of 6 July 2007 to dispense with a criminal investigation and remitted the file for additional investigation.
Instructions were given to question Ms Chelysheva (the ninth applicant) and three named eyewitnesses, to obtain the medical documents and to conduct a forensic examination.

Article 20.2 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that breaches of the established procedure for the organisation of public gatherings, meetings, demonstrations, marches or pickets shall be punishable by an administrative fine of between ten and twenty times the minimum wage, payable by the organisers.

Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that breaches of the established procedure for the conduct of public gatherings, meetings, demonstrations, marches or pickets shall be punishable by an administrative fine of between 1,000 and 2,000 Russian roubles for the organisers, and between 500 and 1,000 Russian roubles for the participants.

Article 27.2 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that the escorting or transfer by force of an individual for the purpose of drawing up an administrative offence report, if this cannot be done at the place where the offence was discovered and if the drawing-up of a report is mandatory, shall be carried out by the police.
Article 27.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that the escort operation shall be carried out as quickly as possible.

Article 27.2 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that the escort operation shall be recorded in an escort operation report, an administrative offence report or an administrative detention report, and that the escorted person shall be given a copy of the escort operation report if he or she so requests.

Article 27.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that administrative arrest or short-term restriction of an individual's liberty may be applied in exceptional cases if this is necessary for the prompt and proper examination of the alleged administrative offence or to secure the enforcement of any penalty imposed by a judgment concerning an administrative offence.

Article 27.3 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that where the detained person so requests, his family, the administrative department at his place of work or study and his defence counsel shall be informed of his whereabouts.

Article 27.3 § 5 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that the arrested person shall have his rights and obligations under the Code explained to him, and the corresponding entry shall be made in the administrative arrest report.
Article 27.4 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that the administrative arrest shall be recorded in a report.
Article 27.4 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that if he or she so requests, the arrested person shall be given a copy of the administrative arrest report.

Article 27.5 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that the duration of the administrative arrest shall not exceed three hours, except in the cases set out in paragraphs 2 and 3 of that Article.

Article 27.5 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that persons subject to administrative proceedings concerning offences involving unlawful crossing of the Russian border may be subject to administrative arrest for up to 48 hours.

Article 27.5 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that persons subject to administrative proceedings concerning offences punishable, among other administrative sanctions, by administrative detention may be subject to administrative arrest for up to 48 hours.

Ms Chelysheva (the ninth applicant) alleged that at Sretenskiye Vorota Square she and other pedestrians had been attacked by a unit of the riot police on 14 April 2007.
Ms Chelysheva (the ninth applicant) alleged that she had seen a policeman hitting a man with a truncheon and had intervened to try to stop the beating.
Ms Chelysheva (the ninth applicant) alleged that a policeman had kicked her on her left leg.
Ms Chelysheva (the ninth applicant) alleged that she had been badly hurt and therefore could not go to the meeting at the Griboyedov monument on 14 April 2007.

On 16 April 2007 Ms Chelysheva (the ninth applicant) filed a complaint with the Moscow prosecutor's office requesting that criminal proceedings be brought against the policemen who had used force against her.
On 6 July 2007 the Meshchanskiy Inter-District Prosecutor's Office decided to dispense with a criminal investigation into the incident involving Ms Chelysheva (the ninth applicant).
On 18 March 2011 the Meshchanskiy Inter-District Prosecutor's Office quashed its decision of 6 July 2007 to dispense with a criminal investigation and remitted the file for additional investigation.
Instructions were given to question Ms Chelysheva (the ninth applicant) and three named eyewitnesses, to obtain the medical documents and to conduct a forensic examination.
Documents submitted by the Government reveal that on 14 April 2007 the Moscow police were reinforced by special units of the riot police (OMON).
The OMON units reinforcing the Moscow police on 14 April 2007 were brought in specially from twenty-nine regions of Russia.
The stated purpose of bringing in OMON units from twenty-nine regions of Russia on 14 April 2007 was "to protect public order and security" on that day.
According to the Government, on 14 April 2007 at about 11.40 a.m. groups of people started gathering near Pushkinskaya Square.
According to the Government, a group of about twenty persons, including the first eight applicants, started marching down Tverskaya Street while shouting anti-government slogans on 14 April 2007.
The applicants claimed that their way had been barred by the riot police who were blocking off several streets in central Moscow on 14 April 2007.

The applicants claimed that all pedestrians, both aspiring protesters and unsuspecting passers-by, had been pushed back, surrounded and indiscriminately beaten up by the riot police before being arrested and taken in police vans to different police stations on 14 April 2007.
